# The Kiln-Stack

You are inside a chimney.

Not a metaphor — or not only one. The space is a vertical bore, perhaps two hundred meters across at its widest and impossibly deep, punched through layers of rock that no one here can name. The walls lean slightly inward as they rise, then lean slightly outward, then lean inward again, so the shaft pulses like a throat. No one has seen the top. No one has seen the bottom. The surveyors who were lowered on cables came back mute, or not at all.

The walls are alive with construction.

---

## The Built Layer

Shelving. That's the first word your mind reaches for. Thousands of platforms, catwalks, balconies, and gantries bolted, wedged, fused, and stacked against the inner walls of the shaft, protruding inward like fungal shelves on a dying tree. The material is mostly slag-ite — a dense, dark ceramicite the color of burnt umber, manufactured somewhere in the lower levels from rawiteite ore that gets hauled up in bucket-elevators that never stop running. The shelves are dense. You cannot move without ducking under a pipe, stepping over a cable, pressing yourself flat against a railing to let someone pass. Every surface has been built upon, built into, built over. Rooms are carved into the wall-rock behind the shelves. Rooms are stacked on rooms. Rooms hang beneath rooms on wire and chain.

The city — and it is a city, though no one calls it that; they call it *the stack* — has no ground. There is no floor. There is only *this level*, *the next level up*, *the level below where the air gets thick*. Navigation is radial and vertical: "four shelves in, seven down," or "outer wall, section twelve, near the big pipe." The big pipe is always audible, a bone-deep hum that you feel in your teeth. It carries something hot and pressurized from the lower reaches to somewhere above. No one shuts it off. No one knows how.

The density is staggering. Every cubic meter that isn't structural has been claimed. Lanterns on hooks. Crates ofite material stacked to the ceiling of a chamber that was already only shoulder-width. Nets strung across open gaps to catch falling tools, falling food, falling people. The shelves creak. The bolts groan. The whole city vibrates faintly, always, from the engines below.

---

## The Engines

They are the industrial heart. Clustered on the middle-depth levels — nobody's sure exactly where the "middle" is; it shifts — the engines are massive piston-and-turbine assemblies, some the size of buildings, bolted directly into the shaft wall. They burniteite dust. The combustion is incomplete and dry: no water is involved in any process here, not in any industrial or biological sense. The exhaust is a fineite mineral particulate that hangs in the air like fog in the lower levels, settling on everything, coating every surface in a thiniteite gray film that people wipe off their eyelids when they wake.

The engines power the elevators, the lights, the smelting furnaces, the compressors, and — crucially — the fans. Without the fans, the air would go dead. The shaft breathes only because it is made to breathe. Massive propellers at irregular intervals push air up and down, creating currents that people read like weather. "Downward blow at section nine" means it's a good time to smoke meat on the upper shelves because the air is clear up there. "Stagnant at the middle" means wear a cloth over your mouth.

Electricity runs through insulated cables — thick black things like arteries — stapled to the wall-rock. The light is dim. Always dim. Fat ceramic bulbs, yellowed and dust-coated, hang from every surface, but they give off a sick, amber half-light that never reaches across the full width of the shaft. The center of the bore is dark. Falling things disappear into that dark. The walls glow. The void does not.

---

## The Life

There are no plants. There is no water. The air carries perhaps three percent humidity on a good day near the upper vents, less elsewhere. And yet the fauna is abundant — teeming, in fact — in every crack and crevice, on every surface, in the walls themselves.

The dominant forms are mineral-arthropod. *Shelless*, the locals call them — creatures whose bodies are compositeiteiteiteiteiteite mineral, calcium-silicate matrices grown in layers like sedimentary rock, with no hydrostatic skeleton, no blood, no moisture to speak of. They move by slow hydraulic expansion: tiny crystalline chambers in their limbs fill with pressurized gas drawn from the ambient air and contract in sequence, producing a slow, deliberate locomotion. They look likeiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteite crabs made ofiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteite concrete. They look likeiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteite walkingiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteite geodes. They look likeiteite nothing you have a word for.

The smallest areiteite dust-mites, barely visible, that coat every surface in a second, living layer atop theiteiteite industrial dust. They feed oniteiteiteiteiteiteiteite mineral particulate — theiteiteiteiteite combustioniteite byproduct — filteringite trace metals from theiteiteite air. They areiteite the base of theiteiteite food chain. Theite larger creatures eat them.

The *shelf-raspers* are the size of a hand, flat-bodied, with filite filament legs that grip any surface. They scrape bioite-film from walls and pipes with mandibles that produce a faint, rhythmic *tik-tik-tik* — one of the few sounds in the otherwise mostly quiet shaft. They cluster in warm areas near the engines, breeding fast, their bodies growing new mineral layers in days. When they grow too heavy for their legs, they fall. They shatter on lower shelves. Other things eat the pieces.

Larger still are the *bore-walkers*, which move up and down the walls on thick, splayed limbs, slow as hour hands. They are the size of dogs, or small goats. Their carapaces are ribbed anditeiteiteiteite dark, blending with the wall-rock. They eat anything — dust-mite aggregations, scrap material,iteiteiteiteite discardediteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteite food packaging,iteite dead shelless creatures,iteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteiteite each other. They have no eyes. They sense vibration through their limbs. The locals leave them alone. They leave the locals alone. An uneasy truce maintained by mutual disinterest.

There are things in the dark center of the shaft, too. You hear them sometimes — a skittering, or a long, slow scraping sound, or something that might be wingbeats if wings were made of slate. No one shines lights into the center. This is not superstition, or not only. The light just isn't strong enough to reach.

## The Atmosphere

Cool. Consistently cool, perhaps eight or nine degrees in the habitable zones, cooler near the upper vents where outside air — if there *is* an outside — seeps in dry and sharp. The air tastesite ofiteiteiteite metal
